mcqs.question: Why can reordering a queue of pending disk requests change total completion time by an order of magnitude on an HDD?
options: Seek time (a few milliseconds per movement) plus rotational latency dominates total time versus actual data transfer, so the order requests are visited in directly determines total head travel
The disk's transfer rate changes depending on request order
Reordering changes how much data each request actually reads
HDDs process requests in parallel, so order never matters
mcqs.explanation: Because seek and rotational latency dwarf transfer time for small/scattered requests, the physical path the head takes between requests is the dominant cost — and that path length depends entirely on visiting order. Transfer rate and request size are unaffected by ordering, and HDDs serve one request at a time, not in parallel.

mcqs.question: A disk request for cylinder 190 sits in the queue while new requests keep arriving near the head's current position around cylinder 20. Under SSTF, what happens to the request at 190?
options: It's serviced immediately regardless of other requests
SSTF automatically promotes old requests after a fixed timeout
It can be starved indefinitely, since SSTF always picks the closest pending request and new nearby arrivals keep winning that comparison
SSTF refuses to accept new requests until the queue is empty
mcqs.explanation: SSTF has no fairness mechanism — it's purely greedy by distance. If closer requests keep arriving, a distant one can wait indefinitely, which is exactly the starvation risk that motivates SCAN-family algorithms. SSTF has no built-in timeout promotion or request-blocking behavior.

mcqs.question: Why does C-SCAN give more uniform wait times across cylinders than plain SCAN?
options: C-SCAN always services requests in numerical order regardless of position

By only sweeping in one direction and jumping back to the start, every cylinder waits roughly one full circular pass — unlike SCAN, where cylinders near the reversal point get serviced twice in quick succession while middle cylinders wait almost a full cycle
C-SCAN eliminates rotational latency entirely
C-SCAN services every request instantly with no wait time
mcqs.explanation: SCAN's back-and-forth sweeping creates uneven wait times because cylinders near a reversal point get two nearby services per cycle while others wait longer. C-SCAN's one-direction-plus-jump-back treats the disk as circular, smoothing this out. It doesn't touch rotational latency or eliminate wait time.

mcqs.question: How does LOOK improve on plain SCAN when pending requests cluster in a narrow band of cylinders far from the disk's physical edges?
options: LOOK reverses direction as soon as no more requests remain ahead in the current direction, avoiding wasted travel all the way to the physical end
LOOK ignores request order entirely and services requests randomly
LOOK only works if requests are evenly spread across the whole disk
LOOK requires twice as many disk heads as SCAN
mcqs.explanation: LOOK's whole improvement is skipping the unnecessary travel to the true physical end of the disk when no requests are out there — it reverses as soon as the current sweep runs out of pending requests ahead of it. It doesn't randomize order, doesn't need even spread, and needs no extra hardware.

mcqs.question: In the worked example (queue [98,183,41,122,14,124,65,67], head at 53), SSTF achieves less total head movement than SCAN. Does this mean SSTF is the better choice for a live production disk scheduler?
options: Yes, lower total movement always means a better algorithm for any workload
No, because the calculation for SSTF in the example is invalid
Yes, but only because the queue size was exactly 8 requests
No — this is a one-shot batch comparison; under continuous request arrival, SSTF's starvation risk for distant requests makes SCAN/LOOK-family algorithms the safer production default
mcqs.explanation: The example is a static snapshot; it can't show SSTF's real-world failure mode of starving distant requests under continuous new arrivals. Production schedulers weigh fairness and worst-case bounds, not just total movement for one fixed batch — which is why LOOK-family algorithms, not raw SSTF, are the standard choice.

mcqs.question: Why does Linux's default I/O scheduler for SSDs (like none or mq-deadline) do far less request reordering than HDD-era schedulers?
options: SSDs cannot handle more than one pending request at a time
Seek-distance minimization has zero benefit on SSDs, since any flash page is electrically addressable in roughly constant time regardless of physical proximity
SSD manufacturers disable scheduling in firmware
mq-deadline is a bug that hasn't been fixed yet
mcqs.explanation: Seek-minimizing logic exists purely to reduce mechanical arm movement, a cost SSDs simply don't have. Reordering by physical proximity is pure overhead with no payoff on flash, so lighter-weight schedulers make sense. SSDs actually handle many parallel requests (the opposite of the first option), and this is deliberate design, not a bug or firmware limitation.
